en: *The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: A Commentary on the Contemplation of the Mind* Composed by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu Jiming.
Having already set forth the meaning of the "truly non-empty," he now expounds it according to Suchness, without grasping or attachment.
"Subsuming those bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, they are fused back into a single thought-moment to form the practice of contemplation.
This "Vajra" is a metaphor for the present single thought-moment of the mind. For example, like a vajra, its substance is the unsurpassed supreme treasure.

In its aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), it is purely immaculate and free from admixture; in its function (*vṛtti*), it is extensively capable of benefiting others. This present single thought-moment is likewise so:
its essence is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), its aspect is unstained by dust, and its function pervades all things. Furthermore, this present single thought-moment is itself the vajra.
While the worldly vajra-treasure takes the mind as a metaphor, it is the worldly treasure that resembles the mind, not the mind that resembles the treasure.

It is the treasure of the world. This present, single thought-moment of the adamantine mind is itself the three kinds of *prajñā*. Its true essence within the *dharmadhātu* is called the "True Aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Its state free from the taints of dust is called "Contemplative Observation" (*vipaśyanā*). Its pervasive application in all functions is called "Letters" (*vyañjana*).
To realize that this single thought-moment possesses the three kinds of prajñā is called a *pāramitā*, because it is the ultimate further shore (*pāra*) of the three virtues.
This nature of the single thought-moment has been constant and unchanging throughout all time, past and present; it serves as a standard and a support;
and because all sages and worthies attain the fruits of the various paths by means of it, it is called a *sūtra*. Furthermore, regarding this present single thought-moment:

This nature has never been different from the beginning; this is called "Suchness" (Tathatā). Beyond this, there is no other dharma; this is called "Reality" (Bhūta). That which universally encompasses and exercises sovereignty is called "Self" (Ātman).

That which clearly seals the objective realm is called "Hearing" (Śruta). That which does not depart from the present thought throughout the ten periods of past and future is called "One Time" (Eka-kṣaṇa).

That which is empty, numinous, and beyond all relativity is called "Buddha. That which vertically exhausts the past and future and horizontally pervades all directions is called "Abiding" (Vartamāna). That which contains, nurtures, and gives birth to all dharmas is called...

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Because he realized that all is but mind, he was able to subdue Māras and externalists; thus he was named "Victorious in Battle" (Jetavana). Because he was a grove of meritorious virtues, it was named "The Tree.

Because his nature was endowed with merit and he provided for all universally, he was named "Sole Provider for the Lonely" (Anāthapiṇḍada). Because it was a gathering place for myriad virtues, it was named "Garden" (Udyāna). Furthermore:
The single thought-moment of the present is, in its very essence, eternally pervasive; this is called "Great" (Mahā). It gives birth to merit and wisdom; this is called a "Bhikṣu.

The mutual correspondence of all minds and mental factors is called the "Assembly" (Saṃgha). A single thought-moment is fully endowed with the ten suchnesses of the hundred realms; this constitutes one thousand.

Its own practice and the transformation of others, with each of the ten wholesome paths mutually inclusive, constitute two hundred. The five faculties and the five powers, each mutually inclusive, constitute fifty. Thus...

Like the ocean seal clearly manifesting [all images], without before or after, it is called "simultaneity" (*yugapat*). Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that transcends the mind; this is called the "World-Honored One.
At all times, one should constantly observe one's own mind; this is called "mealtime. One’s own mind inherently possesses the dharmas of shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and patience (*kṣānti*);
these are called "robes. The harmony and correspondence between the principle and phenomena of one’s own mind is called the "alms bowl. [This applies] throughout the aggregates (*skandha*).

Investigating the principle of the realms and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) is called entering the city to beg for food. Perceiving the principle within each and every phenomenon is called begging in successive order.

Returning to the fundamental principle from the convergence of phenomena is called returning to one's original place. Reaching the ultimate realization of the principle is called having finished eating.
The complete cultivation of practice within the fundamental nature is called "receiving the robes and bowl. The manifestation of merit and wisdom is called "washing the feet.

Realizing the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is called "spreading out the seat and sitting. Furthermore, the mind-factor (*caitta*) that is in accord with [the nature] is called Subhūti.
This understanding possesses a preeminent power and is thus called "Elder" (*sthavira*). Being able to act as the leader among all mind-factors is called "being in the great assembly."
Not grasping at the realization of emptiness is called "rising from one's seat. Following the path of skillful means is called "exposing the right shoulder.

Placing the right knee on the ground signifies that the provisional does not differ from the ultimate; this is called "joining the palms. To observe according to principle is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

To respectfully address the Buddha is called "reverence. That the nature of the mind is inconceivable is called "extraordinary. Immeasurable multitudes of wholesome virtues are called "all Bodhisattvas.

That these wholesome virtues do not depart from the one mind is called "skillfully guarding and mindful of them. That the one mind fully practices all wholesome virtues is called "skillfully entrusting them.
To illuminate the nature in a single thought-moment is called a "good son. To be tranquil in nature in a single thought-moment is called a "good daughter. Relying upon...

The essence of quiescent illumination gives rise to the function of quiescent illumination; this is called "arousing the bodhicitta. When the function accords with the essence, it is called "abiding in accordance [with reality].
To be forever free from obscurity and agitation is called "subduing the mind. Because the rational nature of the mind manifests according to understanding, it is called "the Buddha telling Subhūti:
'Contemplate in accordance with reality. Contemplation itself is in accordance with reality," which is praised as "Excellent, excellent! Furthermore:
The single thought-moment of the present is fully endowed with immeasurable seeds and active manifestations of both defilement and purity;
therefore, it is called "the class of all sentient beings. Being shrouded by ignorance is called "egg-birth" (aṇḍaja). Being concealed and hidden within is called "womb-birth" (jarāyuja).

Moistened by craving and grasping, it is called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*). Manifesting where there is nothing, it is called transformation-born (*upapāduka*). Born from the mind and born as an image, it is called with form (*rūpin*).
Seeking the mind without an image, it is called formless (*arūpin*). Having various objects of perception, it is called with perception (*saṃjñin*).
Grasping at objects without intrinsic nature is called "no-thought. That which is grasped is unreal, thus it is called "not having thought";
yet the grasping subject is not severed, thus it is called "not being without thought. The fundamental nature of ignorance and deluded conceptualization is empty and quiescent;

this is called "nirvana without remainder. To realize that delusion does not arise is called "causing entry into extinction. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are faultless. It is like the removal of a cataract.

The flowers in the sky all vanish; this is called "extinguishing immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Since the nature of the flowers is originally empty, they are not extinguished only now;

this is called "in truth, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction. Within a single thought-moment, one falsely calculates a sovereign self and the continuity of various conditions and forms;
these are called the four marks of selfhood (*ātman* and *dharma*). To be deluded regarding emptiness and calculating them as flowers is called non-Bodhi.

Sā. Furthermore, for the mind to be without the characteristics of mind is called "dwelling nowhere. For thoughts to arise moment by moment is called "activity. Not grasping at a single dharma is called "giving.
Being unstained by a single dharma is called "ethical discipline. Not being obstructed by a single dharma is called "patience.
Not abandoning a single dharma is called "diligence. Not moving a single dharma is called "meditative concentration. Not...
Not obscuring a single dharma is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Not destroying a single dharma is called merit (*puṇya*).

Not perceiving even a single dharma as having the characteristic of limitation or division is called being like empty space. Not reckoning even a single dharma as different from *prajñā* is called abiding according to the teaching.

Furthermore, the essence of the present single thought-moment is the *dharmadhātu*; this is called the non-characteristic of a body. Its original source is true thusness (*tathatā*); this is called suchness.
Come! Because of contemplating the mind, not violating the three karmas is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*). Being upright and gentle is called cultivating merit (*puṇya*).

Because of awakening in a single thought-moment, one is called a "Buddha. When these moments continue in succession until reaching immeasurable thoughts through skillful awakening, this is called planting various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas. The nature of original awakening (*mūlajñāna*) seals, sustains, and encompasses all things.

Because of cultivating virtue, it is called the Tathāgata’s complete knowledge and vision of immeasurable merit. To realize that the mind is signless is called being without the four marks (*catur-nimitta*).
To practice signless goodness is called being without the mark of dharmas (*dharma-nimitta*). To be free from all evil is called being without the mark of non-dharmas (*adharma-nimitta*).

The true analogy for the other shore is wisdom; the raft is the wisdom of contemplation. Abiding securely in the ultimate truth, even the understanding of contemplation is transcended; this is called the Dharma.
One should still relinquish it. Furthermore, the present single thought-moment is itself the Tathāgata, and it is also itself bodhi.

One should not think that the Tathāgata attains the Tathāgata, nor that bodhi attains bodhi. This is because the grasper and the grasped, the speaker and the spoken, are all the very nature of the mind;
since there is neither subject nor object, the nature of this mind is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because all noble sages attain cultivation and realization without departing from the nature of the mind, the presently manifest nature of the mind is itself called the "sūtra.

This Dharma is eternal, for it is subject to no change or decay. Since there are no Buddhas or dharmas of enlightenment that are not established in reliance upon the nature of the mind, if one penetrates the dharma of the mind, one will know the Buddha-dharma and also know all sentient beings.
The Dharma is thus: thirdly, it is without differentiation, for there are no other Buddha-dharmas apart from it. Furthermore, the single thought-moment of the present is itself the Dharma-realm;
because there is neither internal nor external, there is no entering or exiting, nor coming or going, and neither path nor fruit.
Without desire and without detachment, without clamor and without stillness—this is called the practice of the Aranya of the four fruits.
Furthermore, the present single thought-moment, in which light follows light in succession, is called the "Kindled Lamp. That upon which the myriad dharmas rely is called the "Buddha-land.

Pervasive and sovereign, it is called the "Great Body. The object of veneration for the field of merit, it is called the "Stupa and Temple. These three meanings within a single essence are called "Gold."

The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā is the ultimate secret treasury; it is called *pāramitā*. Contemplating the mind according to reality is called "offering" (*bōng*); maintaining this contemplation without loss is called "upholding" (*chí*).

From this point onward, although there are various collections of names, phrases, and syllables, they are subsumed within its meaning and likewise do not depart from the single thought-moment of the present.
This can be understood through the mind; I shall no longer explain them in detail.
Such is the subtle and wondrous meaning of the Vajra: it is not separate from the present single thought-moment.

The *Contemplation of the Mind* (*Xinxin lun*) is fully endowed with the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, and likewise fully endowed with the remaining wondrous scriptures—the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) and the two baskets (*piṭaka*). It even encompasses sūtras as vast in measure as the great trichiliocosm.
Within a single thought-moment, all thoughts are completely dissected; so it is with every other thought as well.
Just as one dissects the Great Sūtra in every moment of thought, so too are all sense faculties and objects dissected.
Until not even the slightest speck of dust remains, there is nothing that does not fully possess the treasury of the Dharma-realm.
Thus, with right wisdom, one should understand that all is but mind;
yet if one does not contemplate the nature of mind, even when the true medicine is present before them, they will not recognize it.
Therefore, I now prostrate in homage to the One who possesses the three virtues by nature, leaving nothing out.
I entreat you one by one to encourage the contemplation of the mind, So that we may swiftly ascend to the Vajra Shore of Prajñā.
The Commentary on the Contemplation of the Mind in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Concluded).
